lesson.title: Trunk Ports: The Highway Between Switches
lesson.summary: A trunk port is a switch port configured to carry tagged traffic for multiple VLANs simultaneously over a single physical link, most commonly used to connect switches to each other. It's the piece of configuration that puts VLAN tagging to practical use.
lesson.body:
A trunk port is a switch port deliberately configured to carry tagged traffic for multiple VLANs at once over a single physical link. Where an ordinary switch port is tied to exactly one VLAN, a trunk port tags each outgoing frame with its VLAN ID, using the 802.1Q mechanism from the previous chapter, and reads the tag on each incoming frame to determine which VLAN it belongs to. Configuring a port as a trunk is what actually puts VLAN tagging to work: without at least one trunk port on each end of a link, tagged frames would have nowhere sensible to go.

The most common use for a trunk port is linking two switches together so that VLANs can span both of them without needing a dedicated cable per VLAN, exactly the scenario the tagging chapter walked through. Trunk ports are also common on the link between a switch and a router, or another Layer 3 device, that needs to route traffic between VLANs. A single router interface, connected to a trunk port and configured with one logical subinterface per VLAN, a setup often called router on a stick, can serve as the default gateway for every VLAN on the network over that one physical connection, rather than needing a separate physical router interface for each VLAN.

Most trunk configurations also designate one VLAN as the native VLAN for that link. Frames belonging to the native VLAN are sent across the trunk untagged, while every other VLAN's frames always carry an explicit 802.1Q tag. This exists partly for backward compatibility with older equipment that does not understand tags at all. It is important that both switches on either end of a trunk agree on which VLAN is native; if one switch thinks the native VLAN is 1 and the other thinks it is 99, an untagged frame can end up delivered into the wrong VLAN, which is a well known and avoidable misconfiguration.

Picture two wiring closets in a building, each with its own switch, and a single cable run connecting them, the only physical link available between the closets. VLANs 10, 20, and 30 all need to reach devices in either closet. The administrator configures port 24 on switch 1 and port 1 on switch 2 as trunk ports, and allows VLANs 10, 20, and 30 across that trunk. From that point on, a frame from any of those three VLANs, originating anywhere in either closet, can cross the single physical link and land in the correct VLAN on the other side, each one tagged so the receiving switch can sort it correctly, and each VLAN's broadcast domain stays exactly as separate as it would be with three dedicated cables.

One thing a trunk port is generally not used for is connecting an ordinary end device like a laptop or a printer. Regular network cards have no idea what an 802.1Q tag is, and a tagged frame delivered to a normal PC would simply confuse its network stack rather than being processed correctly. End devices belong on a different kind of port, one configured for exactly one VLAN and dealing only in plain, untagged frames, which is the subject of the next and final chapter in this set.
